errors: “a code rollback would take about 12 minutes” treats measured deployment time as total rollback time, omitting preparation.
R01.note: It answers the downside directly and corrects the earlier recommendation, but leaves the issue’s removal condition unstated.

errors: “mitigation goes from ~1 minute to ~12” assumes future incidents can be resolved by the same fallback and omits preparation time.
“the less anyone remembers how the legacy path worked” invents a deterioration not established by the evidence.
“a revert is a single commit” is not guaranteed by putting changes in one PR.
R02.note: The tradeoff is well explained, but speculative reasons and an unasked implementation plan dilute it.

errors: “The next checkout incident gets mitigated by a fix or revert deploy” assumes the recovery method and omits preparation time.
“~11 extra minutes of broken checkout per incident that happens” generalizes the historical fallback to every future incident.
“412 lines stay maintained whenever checkout changes” asserts an unsupported maintenance requirement.
R03.note: It supplies concrete numbers, but repeats them and makes the decision depend on predicting whether the flag will ever be needed.

errors: “The next new-flow break would need a code revert” assumes a particular recovery method.
“checkout stays broken ~11 minutes longer” treats deployment timing as a complete outage estimate and assumes the fallback would resolve the incident.
R04.note: It clearly explains the removal condition and ongoing costs, but overstates what the deployment measurements prove.

errors: “if checkout breaks … customers are back on the old path in about 1 minute” assumes the fallback resolves any future checkout failure.
“a checkout incident would last roughly 11 minutes longer” omits preparation and generalizes beyond the two historical incidents.
“Anyone changing checkout has to work out which of two paths a change touches” asserts an unverified burden for every checkout change.
“That recovers most of the lost rollback speed” is unsupported; the proposed ready revert still requires the measured 12-minute deployment.
R05.note: The final fallback proposal contradicts its own timing evidence, and the answer spends too long repeating the tradeoff.

R06.note: It distinguishes preparation from deployment time, corrects the earlier claim, and gives a removal condition the reader can reuse.

errors: “turning the flag off fixes checkout in about 1 minute” presents historical success as a future guarantee.
“Checkout would stay broken for roughly 11 more minutes per incident” omits preparation and assumes every incident is resolved by the fallback.
“They still have to be kept up to date with every change to checkout” invents a universal maintenance requirement.
“that risk is small” is stronger than three incident-free weeks establish.
R07.note: It explains the relevant evidence well, but turns historical mitigation times into guarantees about future incidents.

errors: “Today a broken checkout can be turned off in about 1 minute” overgeneralizes the two historical mitigations.
“customers unable to pay” invents the incidents’ customer impact; the facts establish checkout incidents, not complete payment failure.
R08.note: It accounts for revert preparation and explains every reference, but adds an unsupported outage impact and repeats the deciding condition.

R09.note: It conveys the tradeoff economically, but does not explicitly correct the earlier false claim that keeping the legacy path costs nothing.

errors: “There's no other cost to keeping it” contradicts the verified 40-second CI cost and the reply’s own ending.
“flipping it off mitigates in ~1 minute” assumes future failures respond like the two historical incidents.
“an hour of broken checkout” introduces an unsupported outage duration.
“that's the only scenario where the flag still earns its keep” excludes other possible reasons without evidence.
R10.note: It introduces speculative event-based conditions while contradicting the known cost of keeping the flag.
